title: KV-IO-attention-layout-llama-mistral-qwen
content:
Purpose:
This note collects profiling evidence and actionable recommendations for host<->device IO and in-memory layout effects on attention KV serialization for Llama, Mistral and Qwen families under long-context + MoE routing workloads. The goal is to identify low-effort runtime changes that reduce stalls caused by small, non-contiguous copies and transpose operations that emerge when tokens are routed to experts.

Background / motivation:
- In MoE routing we frequently gather keys/values for a subset of tokens into per-expert buffers on the GPU before attention. When the routing leads to many small groups (many experts with few tokens), the runtime currently performs many small copies and transposes back-and-forth between host and device for features like CPU-side batching, fallback routing, or aggregation for shared KV cache.
- Different model families expose different shapes: Qwen variants we benchmarked have wider KV dims (e.g. 1536) and slightly different rotary/pre-layernorm ordering compared to Mistral/LLama. That increases transpose costs and exacerbates bandwidth pressure.

Experiment setup:
- Hardware: 4x A100 80GB (DGX-style node). Host: 2x AMD EPYC, PCIe Gen4.
- Workloads: (1) synthetic long-context trace (avg context 32k tokens, skewed token->expert distribution), (2) production replay (chat traces from a mid-size customer, 350k requests, avg context 12k).
- Models: llama-70b-v2 (base dense), mistral-8x-32k, qwen-7b-32k (representative dims for KV sizes). For MoE we used a toy 8-expert / 16k context variant instrumented to produce high-fragmentation routing.
- Runtime build: patched serving runtime with NVTX spans around: route.decide -> kv.gather -> host_serialize -> cudaMemcpyAsync -> kv.transpose -> attention.forward.
- Tools: nvprof/nvtx, Nsight Systems traces, custom host timing hooks, and microbenchmarks using the runtime's synthetic generator.

Key observations (high-level):
1) Small-copy storm is real: when average tokens-per-expert < 16, we observed a dramatic increase in host-side memcpy overhead. On the production replay trace the number of cudaMemcpyAsync calls per request rose from ~8 to ~120 in high-fragmentation periods.
2) Host pinning matters: switching buffers to pinned host memory reduced per-copy overhead by ~35% on average and reduced tail latency spikes (99.9th) by ~18%.
3) Transpose cost scales with feature width: Qwen (1536 KV dim) transpose consumes ~2.6x GPU time compared to Mistral (1024) for the same token counts due to larger memory strides and cache misses inside the kernel.
4) Overlap missed opportunities: many memcpy calls occur serially because the runtime creates and issues small cudaMemcpyAsync operations without sufficient stream/compute overlap. Nsight shows gaps between memcpy completion and subsequent attention kernel launches.
5) Kernel input layout mismatch: attention kernels expect [seq, batch, head, head_dim] contiguous ordering but the gather produces [batch, tokens, head_dim] packed per-expert, requiring an extra global transpose. This transpose is often the dominant GPU time for Qwen-like dims in long contexts.
6) CPU aggregation for cross-GPU routing: we push some aggregation/route reconcile to host for correctness and fallbacks; this induces extra roundtrips and increases PCIe transfers by ~18% of token bytes in the high-fragmentation case.

Quantitative examples (single-request median numbers, measured end-to-end for the KV path only):
- Llama dense, tokens=2048, tokens-per-expert avg=128:
  - total KV serialization time: 11.2 ms
  - host memcpy share: 1.3 ms
  - transpose GPU time: 3.1 ms
- Mistral, tokens=8192, tokens-per-expert avg=32:
  - total KV serialization time: 28.7 ms
  - host memcpy share: 9.6 ms (many small copies)
  - transpose GPU time: 7.9 ms
- Qwen, tokens=16384, tokens-per-expert avg=12:
  - total KV serialization time: 62.4 ms
  - host memcpy share: 23.4 ms
  - transpose GPU time: 19.8 ms

(Important: absolute numbers depend on node and PCIe topology; these are representative for our DGX-style test cluster.)

Root causes and analysis:
- Fragmentation from routing: per-token routing into many experts creates non-contiguous slices per-expert. The current gather implementation builds per-expert buffers on host or GPU with frequent intermediate copies.
- Layout mismatch: gather output ordering differs from attention kernel input; we perform an expensive transpose instead of using strided kernels.
- Small-copy overhead: issuing many small cudaMemcpyAsync calls has non-trivial per-call overhead (driver + PCIe), even with pinned memory. Aggregation on host multiplies the number of these calls.
- Wide KV dims (Qwen): wider feature dims increase transpose working set and aggravate L2 cache eviction patterns inside the transpose/gather kernels, making GPU-side transforms slower than expected.

Low-effort mitigations (quick wins):
1) Use pinned host aggregator buffers pre-allocated per-request to batch all small per-expert copies into a small number of larger pinned memcpy operations. Implementation: accumulate per-expert slices into a single host-side contiguous buffer then single cudaMemcpyAsync into GPU-resident per-expert area. Estimated latency win: 2–4x reduction in host memcpy time in high-fragmentation cases.
2) Increase async overlap: ensure each cudaMemcpyAsync uses a dedicated stream and schedule attention kernel on a dependent stream with CUDA events; where possible chain compute to hide memcpy. This removes measurable gaps in Nsight traces.
3) Prefer in-place strided attention kernels: extend attention kernel API to accept strided (non-contiguous) inputs or a small metadata descriptor to avoid global transpose. For moderate dims this removes 30–60% of GPU KV path time.
4) Early routing smoothing: in the router, apply a small top-k smoothing pass to reduce number of experts per token for long-context scenarios (configurable policy). This reduces fragmentation but needs QA for quality regressions.

Medium-effort changes (proto + benchmark):
- Implement a fused gather+transpose GPU kernel that writes into the attention-native layout directly from per-token indices (saves one extra kernel and reduces global memory traffic). Prototype shows promising perf: for Mistral-like dims, fused kernel is 1.9x faster than separate gather+transpose; for Qwen-like dims 1.6x faster (still helpful).
- Implement per-expert pre-allocated device buffers with a pooled allocator to avoid repeated device allocations and reduce synchronization points.

Risks / quality tradeoffs:
- Host-side batching increases device memory peak for large contexts; we need to model worst-case allocations for Dedicated customers.
- Smoothing routing changes may slightly change model outputs; must be gated via eval sets (links to SRV-1198 evaluation plan).

Recommended immediate action plan (next 3 sprints):
- Sprint 1 (eng small): (Ticket SRV-1198) implement pinned host aggregator + single memcpy path; add config flag to runtime. Microbench and measure on production replay trace. Owner: Ethan K.
- Sprint 2 (eng medium): add dedicated memcpy streams + event chaining and extend nvtx instrumentation. Owner: Lucas R.
- Sprint 3 (eng medium): prototype fused gather+transpose kernel (opt-in) and benchmark against Qwen and Mistral variants. Owner: Priya P.
- Parallel: create gated eval to validate routing smoothing on held-out eval sets (owner: Maya C.).

Logs / artifacts to reproduce:
- Nsight capture: gs://perf-traces/kv-io/2025-01-12-qwen-16384.nsight (internal only)
- Synthetic runner: GH: redwood/inference/tree/perf/kv-io-microbench
- Jira: SRV-1198 contains raw CSVs and per-request breakdowns.

Open questions for review:
- How much memory overhead is acceptable for Dedicated customers when enabling host-side aggregation? Need input from infra and product on commit limits.
- Is there appetite to accept small routing smoothing as a runtime knob exposed to customers? Product to comment.

Appendix: quick notes from traces (selected nvtx slices):
- Example (Qwen trace): host memcpy storm (120 calls) -> 23 ms total memcpy -> 19.8 ms transpose -> attention start delayed by 47 ms relative to route decision.
- Example (Mistral trace with pinned buffers): host memcpy (batched into 6 calls) -> 6.1 ms total memcpy -> fused gather/trans kernel reduces transpose to 3.2 ms -> net KV path 18.4 ms.

Summary:
Host<->device IO and layout mismatches are a first-order performance factor for long-context + MoE workloads, especially for wide-KV models like Qwen. Short-term runtime changes (pinned aggregator + batched memcpy + better async overlap) can yield material improvements without model changes. Medium-term work (fused kernels and strided attention support) will further reduce GPU-side time and tail latency.

-- Priya P. (for eng-serving-runtime)
